meta.description: Casey Stengel said it to reporters on 18 October 1960, the day the Yankees dropped him at 70. Wikiquote sources the wording to Joseph Durso's 1967 biography.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I'll never make the mistake of being 70 years old again'?
meta.ogDescription: Real, and dated: Stengel's line at the Yankees press conference of 18 October 1960, when they let him go at 70. Sourced to Joseph Durso's 1967 biography.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1890–1975 · Hall of Fame manager of the New York Yankees and New York Mets
answer.sourceLine: Stengel said it to reporters on 18 October 1960, the day the Yankees put him and co-owner Dan Topping in front of the microphones and ended his twelve years in pinstripes. Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ carries this exact wording — “I guess this means they fired me. I’ll never make the mistake of being 70 years old again” — citing Joseph Durso’s 1967 biography Casey. Beware the variants: the record preserves the joke in at least four slightly different shapes.

source.excerpt: I guess this means they fired me. I’ll never make the mistake of being 70 years old again.
trail: 13 October 1960 — the setup. Bill Mazeroski ends Game Seven of the World Series with a ninth-inning home run and Pittsburgh beats the Yankees 10–9, per the Wikipedia account of the series ↗. It is Stengel’s last World Series as a manager.

18 October 1960 — the press conference. “Five days later, the Yankees called a press conference,” records the SABR biography ↗: co-owner Dan Topping praised Casey’s great work and announced a $160,000 profit-sharing payment; asked whether he had been fired, Stengel said “Write anything you want. Quit, fired, whatever you please. I don’t care”; and then, SABR writes, “he later uttered his famous line.”

19 October 1960 — the front pages. The Detroit Free Press of that date leads with “Yanks Fire ‘Too Old’ Stengel” and carries further coverage inside under “Mighty Casey Strikes Out,” according to the dealer listing for the issue ↗. The press read it as an age story from the first morning.

1967 — the wording is fixed. Joseph Durso’s biography Casey (Prentice-Hall, 211 pp., catalogue record ↗) prints the line, and Wikiquote’s reference chain runs through it. That 1967 text, not a 1960 transcript, is the earliest documentation of this exact phrasing that could be reached for this page.
source.excerptNote: This is the form Wikiquote carries with a reference ↗. The longer version circulating on quote sites — the one that opens “They told me my services were no longer desired because they wanted to put in a youth program” — is held on the article’s talk page ↗ as unsourced, so treat the preamble as unconfirmed.
source.rightsHolder: Joseph Durso / Prentice-Hall for the 1967 biography; the estate of Casey Stengel for his own remarks
source.rightsNote: Stengel spoke the line in October 1960 and the earliest text fixing this exact wording is Joseph Durso’s Casey (Prentice-Hall, 1967) — both far too recent for the US public domain, which currently reaches only works first published before 1931. Quote it with attribution as fair use; it is not free-to-reuse public-domain text.

author.name: Casey Stengel
author.heading: Casey Stengel
author.metaLine: 1890–1975 · Hall of Fame baseball manager · New York Yankees, New York Mets
author.bio: Charles Dillon ‘Casey’ Stengel managed the New York Yankees from 1949 to 1960 and, as Wikipedia ↗ puts it, “won ten pennants in his twelve seasons and won seven World Series” — then took charge of the expansion Mets from 1962 to 1965, a team that finished last all four years. The National Baseball Hall of Fame ↗ credits him with 1,905 wins and 1,842 losses and records that the Yankees dismissed him after the 1960 World Series “citing Stengel’s advancing age.” He was a professional wisecracker as much as a tactician; sportswriters gave his looping, subordinate-clause-strewn manner of speech its own name, Stengelese.

misattribution.heading: Not the wrong man — the wrong words
misattribution.intro: Nobody else is credited with this line; the problem is that no two sources say it the same way. Stengel spoke it once, off the cuff, to a room full of reporters filing on deadline, and the sentence has been drifting ever since. Here is what actually varies.

items.why: Turning, not being. This is the form used in the Wikipedia article on the 1960 World Series ↗. It changes the joke slightly — from an ongoing state to a one-off act.

items.who: “…the mistake of being seventy again” / “…of being 70 again”
items.why: The SABR biography ↗ gives “being seventy again”; SABR’s own journal piece “The Remaking of Casey Stengel” ↗ gives “being 70 again.” Both drop the “years old” that Wikiquote’s sourced text keeps.

items.who: “They told me my services were no longer desired because they wanted to put in a youth program…”
items.why: Quote aggregators routinely bolt this preamble onto the punchline and present the whole thing as one utterance. Wikiquote does not treat it as sourced: the combined version sits on the article’s talk page ↗ among quotes flagged as needing citation, while only the short form appears in the article with a reference.

misattribution.truthLine: The joke is genuinely Stengel’s and genuinely from 18 October 1960. If you want a form you can defend, use the one Wikiquote actually sources ↗ to Durso’s 1967 biography: “I guess this means they fired me. I’ll never make the mistake of being 70 years old again.”

context.heading: Why the line landed
lead: The Yankees had just lost the 1960 World Series in the most spectacular way available: on 13 October, Bill Mazeroski hit a walk-off home run in the bottom of the ninth of Game Seven, and Pittsburgh won 10–9. Five days later the club called a press conference. Co-owner Dan Topping talked about Casey’s great work and about a $160,000 profit-sharing payment, and never quite said the word. When reporters pressed, Stengel refused to help them: “Write anything you want. Quit, fired, whatever you please. I don’t care.” Then he handed them the headline anyway.

The joke works because it isn’t self-pity — it’s a man taking the organisation’s stated reason and repeating it back as an absurdity. The Yankees had said they wanted a youth programme. Stengel, seventy years old and holding ten pennants from twelve seasons, agreed that his age was the offence and promised not to repeat it. That is the whole grammar of Stengelese in one sentence: a straight face over a knife.
detailsBody: He was not done. In 1962 Stengel came back across town to manage the brand-new New York Mets, and stayed through 1965 — four seasons in which, as Wikipedia notes, the team “finished last all four years he managed it.” The Yankees, meanwhile, won the pennant in 1961 and 1962 under Ralph Houk.
The Hall of Fame elected him in 1966. He died on 29 September 1975.
context.pull: “Write anything you want. Quit, fired, whatever you please. I don’t care.”

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's sourced Casey Stengel section contains the exact wording "I guess this means they fired me. I'll never make the mistake of being 70 years old again," cited to Joseph Durso's 1967 biography Casey; the life and legend of Charles Dillon Stengel, reproduced in Ed Rumill, "'Casey': A Career in Stengelese," The Christian Science Monitor, 19 April 1967, p. 13. The page has no Misattributed or Disputed section.

The Wikiquote talk page lists the longer combined version — "They told me my services were no longer desired because they wanted to put in a youth program as an advance way of keeping the club going. I'll never make the mistake of being seventy again." — among quotes without citation attribution, i.e. unsourced.

SABR's BioProject life of Casey Stengel states "Five days later, the Yankees called a press conference," reports Dan Topping praising Casey's work and a $160,000 profit-sharing payment, quotes Stengel's "Write anything you want. Quit, fired, whatever you please. I don't care," and says "He later uttered his famous line, 'I'll never make the mistake of being seventy again.'"
SABR's journal article "The Remaking of Casey Stengel" quotes the line in the context of the 1960 firing as: "I'll never make the mistake of being 70 again," he said.

Wikipedia's 1960 World Series article states Game 7 was played 13 October 1960, that Pittsburgh beat New York 10–9 on Bill Mazeroski's ninth-inning home run, and renders Stengel's remark as "I'll never make the mistake of turning 70 again."

Wikipedia's Casey Stengel article gives his dates as born 30 July 1890 and died 29 September 1975, states his Yankees teams "won ten pennants in his twelve seasons and won seven World Series" (1949–1960), that he managed the Mets 1962–1965 and the team "finished last all four years he managed it," and that "By then aged 70, he was dismissed by the Yankees shortly after their defeat."

The National Baseball Hall of Fame profile gives Stengel's managerial record as 1,905 wins and 1,842 losses (.508) over 3,766 games and states the Yankees dismissed him after the 1960 World Series "citing Stengel's advancing age." It does not itself quote the "70" line.
Open Library's record for the work confirms Casey: the life and legend of Charles Dillon Stengel by Joseph Durso, published 1967 by Prentice-Hall, Englewood Cliffs, N.J., 211 pages.

The RareNewspapers listing is for the Detroit Free Press of 19 October 1960, whose front page ran the headline "Yanks Fire 'Too Old' Stengel" with further coverage on page 33 headed "Mighty Casey Strikes Out."

ThisGreatGame's 1960 baseball history page states the press conference took place on 18 October, that Dan Topping announced Stengel's firing and a $160,000 payment "to do with as he pleases," and quotes Stengel: "I'll never make the mistake of being 70 again."

Harvey Frommer's "You Could Look It Up" piece renders the passage as "They told me that my services were no longer desired because they wanted to put in a youth movement as an advance way of keeping the club going" and "Most guys my age are dead at the present time anyway and you could look it up. I'll never make the mistake of being seventy years old again." — a further wording variant.

NEGATIVE CONTROL: Quote Investigator has no article on this quote. Site-restricted searches for the phrase returned no quoteinvestigator.com result, so no QI anchor exists to defer to and none is cited.
